subject: sunk-cost
title: The Ticket You Already Paid For
summary: Money you already spent is gone. Why it should not boss around your next choice.

keys.answer: Money, time or effort you already spent and cannot get back.

options.text: Something you already spent and cannot get back
Money you plan to spend next week
Money you will get back later

keys.prompt: Why shouldn't a sunk cost decide what you do next?
keys.answer: It is gone no matter what you pick. Only what happens next can still change.

options.text: It is gone no matter what you pick
It always means you should quit
It comes back if you keep going

keys.prompt: Does skipping the sunk cost trap mean you should always quit?
keys.answer: No. If going on is still worth it from now on, keep going.

options.text: No, keep going if it is still worth it from now on
Yes, always quit right away
Yes, but only on weekends

cards.title: Two tickets, one weekend
cards.text: Imagine you have two tickets for the same day. One cost a lot. The other cost less, but it sounds way more fun. You can only use one. Which would you pick? Lots of people pick the one that cost more.

cards.question: College students imagined a $100 ski trip and a $50 ski trip on the same weekend. They thought the $50 trip would be more fun. Which trip did more of them pick?

options.text: The $50 trip, since it was more fun
The $100 trip
Exactly half picked each one

cards.reveal: More picked the $100 trip: 33 students. Only 28 picked the $50 trip they thought was more fun.

cards.title: Money that is already gone
cards.text: A sunk cost is something you already spent and cannot get back. It can be money, time or effort. Whatever you pick next, that money stays spent. So it should not decide what you do next.
cards.example: Go or stay home, a ticket you paid for is paid either way.

why.q: Why shouldn't money you already spent decide what you do next?
why.a: It is gone no matter what you pick. Only what happens next can still change.

cards.title: The ski trip puzzle
cards.text: In a study from 1985, college students imagined two ski trip tickets for the same weekend. One cost $100. The other cost $50, and they thought it would be more fun. They could use only one. 33 students picked the $100 trip. Only 28 picked the more fun one!

cards.title: A test with real tickets
cards.text: Then the scientists tried it for real at a college theater. Some people paid the full $15 for a whole season of plays. Others got a surprise discount of $2 or $7. In the first half of the season, the full-price group went to more plays. Paying more made them go more.

cards.title: A plane faster than sound
cards.text: Britain and France built Concorde, a jet that flew faster than sound. It cost a huge amount. Even when it was clear the plane would not make money, they kept paying. Now people sometimes call this trap the "Concorde fallacy."

cards.title: Look forward, not back
cards.text: Smart choosers look only at what happens from now on. That does not mean you should always quit. If going on is still worth it, keep going! Just don't keep going only because you already paid.
cards.example: Say your movie ticket is paid, and then friends ask you to play soccer, which you love even more. The money is gone either way, so pick the one that will be more fun.

cards.question: Is there something you keep doing only because you already put time into it? If you were starting fresh today, would you pick it again?
nudges: Think about a game, a book, a show or a hobby.
What would happen next if you kept going? What if you stopped?

options.text: Money or time already spent that you cannot get back
options.why: Yes! It is spent, and it is not coming back.

options.text: Money you plan to spend next week
options.why: Not quite. That money is not spent yet, so you can still choose.

options.text: Money you will get back later
options.why: Not quite. A sunk cost is money you cannot get back.

questions.q: In the theater test, who went to more plays in the first half of the season?

options.text: People who paid full price
options.why: Right! Paying more made people go more.

options.text: People who got a $7 discount
options.why: Not quite. The discount groups went to fewer plays.

options.text: Everyone went the same amount
options.why: Not quite. The groups were different, and price was the only change.

questions.q: Your family paid for a fair, but a big storm starts. What is the smart way to think?

options.text: The money is gone either way, so pick what is best now
options.why: Yes! Think about what happens from now on.

options.text: We paid, so we must go no matter what
options.why: That is the sunk cost trap. The money is gone either way.

options.text: We should never buy tickets again
options.why: Not quite. Buying tickets is fine. Just choose well later.

sources.title: Sunk cost
sources.supports: A sunk cost is a cost already paid that cannot be recovered and should not matter for decisions about the future; only future consequences matter; continuing a project can still be right when its future value is high enough (the factory example); the British and French governments kept funding the costly supersonic Concorde after there was no economic case, which is why it is called the "Concorde fallacy".

sources.title: The Psychology of Sunk Cost
sources.publisher: Arkes & Blumer, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 35 (1985), PDF copy
sources.supports: Experiment 1 (Ohio and Oregon college students): $100 Michigan ski trip vs $50 Wisconsin trip thought to be more enjoyable, same weekend, only one usable; 33 chose the $100 trip and 28 the $50 trip. Experiment 2: Ohio University Theater 1982–1983 season tickets at $15, $2 off or $7 off, assigned at random; the no-discount group used more tickets in the first half of the season. Sunk costs can be money, effort or time.
